sentences.text: The hut was set back about fifty meters from the beach, on a small rise, surrounded by low wind-bent birches.
It was very old — the wood was silver-grey, almost black in places, and the roof was moss and old wooden shingles.
There was one door and one small window.
Priit lifted the wooden latch, which was heavy and stiff, and pushed the door open.
They fell inside, wet, both breathing hard, and Priit closed the door behind them and dropped the latch.
Inside, it was dim, dry, and smelled of old wood and dry pine sap and, faintly, of woodsmoke a long time gone.
Kaarel wiped water out of his eyes and looked around.
It was a small square room, maybe three meters by three.
A rough wooden bench along one wall, wide enough to lie on.
A small wood stove in the corner, cold.
A wooden table under the window.
A shelf on the back wall with a few empty tins and a very old iron kettle.
And, hanging from a hook in the low ceiling right above the door, a small bronze bell about the size of a man's fist, with a thin dark rope tied to its clapper.
The rope went up to the bell, and then went sideways, and disappeared through a tiny hole drilled in the wall just under the roofline.
Kaarel stared at the bell.
Priit went to the stove.
Beside it, in a small neat pile, was dry kindling and half a dozen split birch logs.
There was a small tin on top of the stove.
Priit opened it — three dry matches.
He looked pleased.
He built a small careful fire, lit the match, and after a moment the stove began to warm.
He set the iron kettle on top and put water from his emergency bottle into it.
He said, "We will have tea in ten minutes.
Then it will feel less bad."
Kaarel sat on the wooden bench, wrapped in the old blanket from the emergency bag, and watched.
When Priit was done fussing with the fire, Kaarel asked, "Who left the wood and the matches?" Priit said, "Whoever used the hut last.
It is a rule.
If you use a storm hut, you leave it better than you found it.
Dry wood.
Dry tinder.
Matches if you can spare them.
Someone might come after you who does not have time to gather." He looked at his son.
"When we leave, we will do the same.
We will refill the kindling from the shed outside.
That is how this works."
The rain drummed hard on the mossy roof.
The wind rose and rose.
Kaarel could hear the sea outside — a heavier sound than that morning, a deep booming somewhere off to the north where the waves were breaking on the exposed side of the islet.
But inside the hut it was warm and dry and very quiet in the way small warm places are quiet in a storm.
Kaarel drank the tea Priit made him — hot and strong and with too much sugar from a small paper packet in the emergency bag.
He began to feel less afraid.
"Whose hut was this?" he asked.
Priit said, "The Nurmis.
My grandfather's family — your great-grandfather's family.
They were fishermen.
They lived on this islet for four hundred years.
There were maybe fifteen of them here at the peak.
They left in the thirties.
My great-uncle Toivo was the last brother out.
He walked away from the door of this hut in nineteen thirty-eight and closed it and rowed to Saaremaa and never came back.
I met him once when I was small.
He died when I was eight."
Kaarel looked around the small dim room.
He said, "So who's been keeping the wood?" Priit thought.
He said, "Other people.
Fishermen.
There is always someone.
On the Väinameri, someone always keeps the storm huts stocked.
Nobody organizes it.
It just happens.
It is like the bell, I suppose." And he looked up at the bronze bell hanging over the door.
The storm did not stop.
If anything, in the evening, it got heavier.
Priit checked the boat once, at dusk, and came back to say it was still tied and fine but the water had come up higher than he had expected.
"Not dangerous," he said, "but higher than normal.
We will sleep here.
There will be nothing to do until the wind drops.
If we are lucky, it drops by morning." He gave Kaarel more tea, and one of the two sandwiches from the emergency bag.
They ate.
They talked a little.

Priit told Kaarel about his great-uncle Toivo, who had been a quiet strange man who had lived alone on the mainland for the rest of his life and who had never once, in fifty years, gone back to Kesselaid.
Kaarel asked why.
Priit said, "I do not know.
Something happened here.
My father would not tell me."
The fire burned down slow.
Priit rolled up his jacket for a pillow and lay down on the floor.
He gave Kaarel the whole bench and the blanket.
Within a few minutes he was asleep.
He always slept easily.
Kaarel lay on the bench and listened to the rain and looked at the shape of the bell hanging overhead in the dim red glow of the coals.
Then, at some point, he slept too.
He did not know what time it was when he woke up.
It was still full dark.
The rain had softened — no longer heavy — and the wind had dropped some.
The fire was down to a warm red.
And the bell above the door was ringing.
Not loud.
A slow, uneven, quiet ding-ding.
Pause.
Ding.
Pause.
Ding-ding.
As if something outside was pulling the rope, once, and then once again, and then twice.
Kaarel sat up on the bench.
His heart was beating fast.
He looked at his father, who was still asleep and breathing evenly.
Priit had not heard it.
The bell rang again — slow, patient, almost polite.
Kaarel got up very quietly, wrapped in the blanket, and crossed the small room to the door.
